title: MoE routing context-sensitivity and cross-model latency probes
content:
Summary:
This note collects lightweight experiments and hypotheses about how MoE routing interacts with long-context workloads across three representative architectures (LLaMA-family, Mistral variants, and Qwen). The goal is to understand why p95 token latency and tail variance rise non-linearly as context grows in certain workloads and to propose low-effort mitigations to test in the runtime.

Motivation / why this matters now:
- Multiple customer workloads (search summarization, multi-turn dialogue) show intermittent ~2–5× p95 increases when context > 4k tokens on MoE-backed models.
- Observed spikes correlate with routing decisions that cause different expert sets to be activated across close-by requests, increasing kernel churn and memory pressure.
- We need concrete, reproducible probes that differentiate: kernel-selection overhead, KV-cache thrash, expert memory reallocation, and scheduler inefficiencies.

Experimental setup (simple, reproducible):
- Hardware: single A100-80GB (shared test pool), additional probes on 2xA40 for comparison.
- Runtime: v0.42 branch with tracing enabled (lightweight counters + per-op time).
- Models: LLaMA-13B-MoE (2-4 expert shards), Mistral-7B variant with MoE layer adaptions, Qwen-14B-MoE experimental.
- Prompts: three synthetic families: "stable-prefix" (same prefix repeated across calls), "slightly-shifted" (prefix token offset by 1–3 tokens), "content-drift" (semantically different prefix but same token-length distribution).
- Context lengths tested: 512, 2048, 4096, 8192 (where supported).
- Metrics captured: per-token latency p50/p95/p99, kernel count (unique kernels launched per request), allocation/deallocation counts, KV-cache hit ratio, routing entropy (Shannon over expert selection), memory high-water mark.

Key observations (high level):
1) Kernel-launch and small-kernel overheads matter at long contexts:
   - LLaMA-family paths stay relatively stable up to 4k; p95 rises by ~1.4× at 8k. Kernel diversity is small (attention + ff only).
   - Mistral variants show earlier tails (p95 2× at 4k) driven by attention kernel decomposition used for rotary/ALiBi handling in our optimized path — leads to extra kernel calls per layer.
   - Qwen-MoE had the highest kernel churn in "slightly-shifted" experiments: small prefix shifts change memory layouts and cause additional kernel rebinds.

2) MoE routing entropy correlates with tail latency spikes:
   - Requests in the "content-drift" family produce higher routing entropy -> more unique experts touched across the request set -> more frequent expert tensor allocations and cross-expert swap activity.
   - When routing entropy crosses ~1.2 bits per token (empirical threshold in our tests), p95 jumps sharply. This suggests amortization breaks: cost of touching extra experts is not negligible vs. compute saved.

3) KV-cache interaction with MoE leads to sub-optimal reuse:
   - We observe cases where the same logical sequence produces different expert activations between generation steps (gating sensitivity), which in turn maps to different KV-cache keys (internal layout differs) causing cache misses and recompute of prefix context.
   - Cache miss penalty is heavier on long contexts because recomputing prefix contribution requires many attention passes; net effect: cache miss latency ~ proportional to prefix length.

4) Memory / allocator pressure and kernel fragmentation:
   - Small, frequent tensor allocations (per-expert temp buffers) increase allocator overhead. On A100 we measure ~8–12% extra CPU-side time waiting for allocations under high routing churn.
   - On multi-socket setups where experts are sharded, cross-device movement (fallbacks) causes costly NCCL/PCIe traffic spikes and scheduler backpressure.

Representative micro-benchmarks (median of repeated runs):
- LLaMA-13B-MoE, stable-prefix, context=2048: p50 ~ 30ms/token, p95 ~ 55ms/token.
- LLaMA-13B-MoE, content-drift, context=8192: p50 ~ 65ms/token, p95 ~ 140ms/token.
- Mistral-7B, slightly-shifted, context=4096: p50 ~ 28ms/token, p95 ~ 96ms/token (attention kernel multiplicity).
- Qwen-14B-MoE, slightly-shifted, context=2048: p50 ~ 42ms/token, p95 ~ 180ms/token (kernel churn + allocator waits).
(Absolute numbers are environment dependent; use as relative signal.)

Profiling traces / hotspots (where to look in runtime):
- Per-layer gate evaluation (CPU->GPU handoff) timing: high variance here indicates gating busy-wait or copy overhead.
- Expert dispatch tensor reshapes and per-expert launch loops: look for small launches that could be batched.
- KV-cache key normalization code path: differences in layout between experts lead to branching.
- Attention kernel selection code (kernel_picker): document cases where we pick decomposed kernels for Mistral and avoid them for LLaMA for same seq_len.

Hypotheses (causal chains to validate):
A) Routing jitter hypothesis: small differences in tokenization/prefix cause gate top-k shifts, which produce different expert sets -> additional allocations + kernel launches -> latency tail.
B) Cache-compatibility hypothesis: our KV-cache key is sensitive to per-layer expert mapping; when expert sets differ across steps, cache keys mismatch and we pay redos.
C) Kernel-fragmentation hypothesis: the runtime launches many small kernels when experts are sparse, incurring non-trivial launch overhead that grows with number of experts touched per request.

Low-effort mitigations to try (ordered by implementation friction):
1) Gate-stabilization: increase gating temperature smoothing (simple EMA over gate logits for the first N tokens) to reduce hopping on short shifts. Risk: small quality regression.
2) Cheap per-request expert pinning: if routing entropy > threshold, pin top-2 experts for the entire request to reduce allocation churn. Simple runtime flag; evaluate quality.
3) Consolidated expert buffers: pre-allocate per-expert scratch buffers in a pool to avoid per-request allocations. Avoids allocator overhead.
4) KV-cache normalization layer: add expert-agnostic normalization to cache key generation so that logically-equivalent states map to same key even if expert mapping differs. Moderate complexity.
5) Kernel fusion for small-expert batches: batch small expert workloads into one fused kernel when possible (higher engineering cost).

Proposed next experiments (short runs we can schedule this week):
- A/B test Gate-stabilization with 10% of traffic for two customer workloads; measure delta p95 and quality (perplexity + spot-check completions).
- Run controlled microbench where we pin experts artificially vs native gating, measure allocation counts and kernel-launch counts.
- Add brief tracepoint in KV-cache path that records cache key fingerprint + expert_map fingerprint to quantify cache-mismatch rate.

Open questions / risks:
- Quality impact of expert pinning and gate smoothing is unknown; need to run automated evals to detect regression.
- Some mitigation (kernel fusion, consolidated buffers) move complexity into allocator/kernel codepaths and may affect other non-MoE models.
- Multi-tenant environments may have different memory pressure dynamics; tests on larger clusters needed.

Notes on model-specific quirks (quick bullet list):
- LLaMA-family: generally stable gating, lower kernel diversity. Biggest pain is KV-cache recompute cost at 8k+.
- Mistral-family: attention decomposition increases kernel count; works well when prefix is stable but degrades with small shifts due to rebinds.
- Qwen-family: tokenization differences + internal chunking make small prefix shifts more likely to change memory layouts; gating interacts badly with that.

Conclusions (short):
- Tail latency on MoE long-context workloads is multi-factor: routing entropy, KV-cache mismatches, kernel-launch fragmentation, and allocator pressure.
- Low-friction mitigations (gate smoothing, expert pinning, consolidated buffers) are promising and should be validated quickly.
- Allocate 2 engineer-weeks to implement tracepoint + gate-stabilization prototype and run customer A/B tests.

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducible test run
- checkout serving-runtime@profiling/moe-context-v2
- enable --trace-gating --trace-kvkeys flags
- run harness with seeds [42,314,7], request families described above, collect 50 runs per config
- dump per-request JSON traces to s3://redwood-bench/moe-context/DATE
